clue.text: Cool cat is into playing the violin, OK?

indicators.note: one thing being into another means it sits inside it, so the first pair goes within the playing phrase

parts.note: playing the violin is fiddling
to air something is to cool it
a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: A laid-back jazz cat asks whether his fiddle playing is acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is into' signals the container. 'Cool cat' looks like jazz slang for one person, but it gives two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean middling or passable, so the colloquial phrase is a fair substitute for a questioning 'all right?'

clue.text: Universal? Exactly

definitions.meaning: applying everywhere on earth, said of something worldwide
used in comparisons like 'looking just like', meaning precisely

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase can mean throughout the globe, and in 'for all the world like' it means precisely.

clue.text: Slapping paint on, and gone in one second

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I

indicators.note: gone sits inside the word for a second

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second
gone means past, over

explanation.surface: A painter slaps paint on quickly, and it's all over in a second.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals the container; 'one second' reads as a single time span but splits into the numeral and a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: The art term names paint laid on thickly so brush strokes stand out, which is what slapping it on produces.

clue.text: Plod endlessly round east, sporting ' wide-brimmed hat

indicators.note: the cut word goes round the east letter, enclosing it
endlessly means the final letter of the trudging word is dropped

parts.note: to trail is to walk wearily, to plod

explanation.surface: A trudging walker heads east wearing a broad-brimmed sun hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts TRAIL to TRAI and 'round' puts it around E. 'Plod' tempts as the slang for a policeman; here it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A double-crowned felt hat with a wide brim, worn in hot countries and named after an Indian lowland region.

clue.text: Fool dipped articles in sea

indicators.note: something dipped is lowered into liquid, so the articles go inside the sea
with dipped, in says where the articles are placed: inside the sea

parts.note: the Med is the Mediterranean Sea
the articles a, the and a again

explanation.surface: Some idiot dunked a few things in the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dipped ... in' puts the articles A, THE, A inside MED, the Mediterranean.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial insult for a stupid person, an idiot.

clue.text: Fancies a maiden wearing short frock

indicators.note: the frock is worn around the girl, so it encloses those letters
short means the last letter of the frock word is dropped

parts.note: a frock is a dress
M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A girl in a short frock has romantic fancies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' cuts DRESS to DRES; 'wearing' puts A and M inside it. A maiden over in cricket is one with no runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreams are fancies or fantasies, idle imaginings; both are plural nouns.

clue.text: Craftswoman's place in South Africa

definitions.meaning: a smith is a metalworker, and a female one could be called a ...
a town in KwaZulu-Natal, famous for its siege in the Boer War

explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it names a female metalworker; as one it is the besieged South African town.

clue.text: Stripling gets engaged, saving up money for the future

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from bottom to top
saving here means keeping inside, so the letters sit within the words

explanation.surface: A young man gets engaged and starts putting money aside for married life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'saving' takes GGETSEN from stripLING GETS ENgaged and 'up' turns it round. The comma hides that 'saving up' is the indicator, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sum of savings set aside for later use is called a nest egg.

clue.text: Don't be ashamed to detain the teacher in charge

parts.note: to hold up is to detain or delay
the head is the teacher in charge of a school, so one's head

explanation.surface: Someone is told not to feel bad about keeping the headteacher back.
explanation.walkthrough: HEAD, short for headteacher, is the teacher in charge of a British school.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to keep your dignity and refuse to feel shame.

clue.text: News presentation about movement of boat cargo

parts.note: re means about, concerning
portage is carrying boats and goods overland between waters

explanation.surface: A news item covers the shifting of a ship's freight.
explanation.definitionFit: Reporting of news events, especially by journalists, is reportage.

clue.text: Type of music is featured in retro recording, old

indicators.note: is appears inside the turned recording, as a feature within it
retro means backwards, so the recording abbreviation is read in reverse

parts.note: a CD is a compact disc recording

explanation.surface: A kind of music appears on an old retro record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retro' signals the reversal and 'featured in' the container; 'old' is added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A style of dance music popular in the 1970s, a genre.

clue.text: Girl and I meet for a drink

parts.note: a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: A young woman and I get together over a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: An Indian yogurt-based beverage, sweet or salty.

clue.text: Badly made paths in part of London

indicators.note: badly made means these letters are wrongly assembled, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Poorly laid footpaths in a London district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' rearranges MADE PATHS.
explanation.definitionFit: A district in north London, home of the Heath.

clue.text: West-facing coastal town, one close to California, hot and humid

indicators.note: in an across clue facing west means reading right to left, backwards

parts.note: a port is a coastal town
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A seaside town looking west, near California, has sultry weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West-facing' signals the reversal in an across clue; 'close to' simply means next to.
explanation.definitionFit: The climate of the tropics is typically hot and humid.

clue.text: Function at home: fellow entertains old lady

parts.note: in means at home

indicators.note: a host entertains guests inside, so the fellow encloses the old lady

parts.note: Ted is a man's name, standing for any fellow
gran is a grandmother, an old lady

explanation.surface: A function held at home where a man entertains an elderly woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entertains' signals the container: the host holds the guest inside.
explanation.definitionFit: In calculus, the function being integrated is called the integrand.

clue.text: Try to contact group of people at university

parts.note: a ring is a group of people, often a criminal one
to be up is to be in residence at university

explanation.surface: Attempting to reach a bunch of students.
explanation.walkthrough: Being UP means in residence at a British university, especially Oxford or Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: To ring up is to telephone, an attempt to contact someone.

clue.text: Supermarkets' leader: new, cheaper fish

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter
new means the letters are made into something new, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: The top supermarket advertises a new cheaper fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' takes S; 'new' rearranges CHEAPER into EAPERCH.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea perch is any of various marine fish resembling the freshwater perch.

clue.text: Number of some importance, though not initially

indicators.note: not initially means the first letter is removed

parts.note: weighty means important, significant

explanation.surface: A figure that matters, though not at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not initially' drops W from WEIGHTY.
explanation.definitionFit: A cardinal figure, four score.

clue.text: There's a good boy — study, please

parts.note: a lad is a boy
a den is a study, a private room

explanation.surface: Praising a well-behaved boy and asking him to study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'please' looks like a polite request but is a verb, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To gladden someone is to make them happy, to please them.

clue.text: Came across a teacher swallowing hard drug

indicators.note: the swallower takes the hard letter inside

parts.note: met means came across, encountered
a don is a university teacher
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Bumping into a lecturer who downs a strong narcotic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swallowing' puts H inside METADON. 'hard drug' looks like one phrase, but 'hard' gives H.
explanation.definitionFit: A synthetic opioid used to treat heroin addiction; usually spelt with a final E, which this spelling drops.

clue.text: Radio expert blows his top investigating broken radio set

indicators.note: the one investigating is placed inside the broken set
broken means the letters of the word are smashed and reassembled
losing his top means the first letter of the expert is removed

parts.note: a radio ham is an amateur radio expert

explanation.surface: A radio buff loses his temper while looking into a broken wireless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blows his top' signals beheading, 'broken' the anagram (giving DIORA) and 'investigating' the container, placed before the final A. A radio ham is an amateur radio enthusiast.
explanation.definitionFit: A diorama is a model scene, a three-dimensional set.

clue.text: Man: a northern isle

parts.note: to man is to staff, as in crewing a post

explanation.surface: Introducing a man from an island in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' tempts as the Isle of Man; it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A small island in the Inner Hebrides of Scotland, known for Fingal's Cave.

clue.text: In apron somehow catch one butterfly

indicators.note: the pieces go in the rearranged word
somehow means the letters are put together in some other way

parts.note: to get is to catch
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone tries to catch a butterfly using their apron.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' signals the anagram (giving ORANP) and 'In' the container, placed before the final P.
explanation.definitionFit: A European butterfly, the males having orange wing tips.

clue.text: Religious prior expels reverend

indicators.note: expels means the reverend's letters are thrown out of the longer word

parts.note: prior means previous

explanation.surface: A devout prior throws out a clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'expels' removes REV from PREVIOUS. 'prior' looks like the head of a priory but means earlier.
explanation.definitionFit: Pious means devoutly religious.

parts.note: the clue 4 answer read as two words describes a meat paste that also means heads; plural both ways

explanation.definitionFit: Pates are heads, and the accented spelling names a meat spread, so the plural fits both readings.

clue.text: Female troubled daily

indicators.note: troubled letters are disturbed, so they get rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman who is upset every day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troubled' rearranges DAILY.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name; a female name stands for any female.

clue.text: Topping tipped over pastries, then put in to bake

indicators.note: the turned pastries are put into the baking word

parts.note: to fire is to bake, as with pottery in a kiln

indicators.note: tipped over means turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: tarts are pastries

explanation.surface: A dessert topping knocked over onto pastries, which then go in the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tipped over' signals the reversal (giving STRAT) and 'put in' the container. 'Topping' looks like a dessert garnish but is old slang for excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Topping is old slang for excellent, top-notch.

clue.text: Oscar's best mate?

parts.note: Oscar is Oscar Wilde; a best mate read as a perfect spouse is the title of one of his comedies

explanation.definitionFit: The 1895 Wilde comedy's title describes a perfect spouse, a best possible mate.
